# Customer interview: home goods importer

Recorded: 18 March 2026. Video call, transcript with timestamps, lightly cleaned.
Interviewee: Tom Hadley, director of Hadley & Finch Home Ltd

---

\[00:00:09\] **Tom, thanks for making the time. Could you start by telling me what the business does?**

yeah, sure. so basically we import kitchen and home stuff from China and sell it online, mostly on Amazon, and we've got our own little store on Shopify as well. the company's Hadley & Finch Home Ltd, we're based in Leeds, warehouse is just outside Bradford. and about two years ago we opened a US arm, Hadley Home Goods LLC, registered in Austin, because the US market is just, you know, ten times bigger. bamboo chopping boards, spice racks, those collapsible silicone bowls, that kind of thing. nothing glamorous but it sells.

\[00:01:20\] **How did you get into it in the first place?**

honestly, by accident. I was working in logistics, hated it, and a mate of mine, Robbo, well, Rob Ashdown, he was already flipping phone cases on eBay. he said, mate, it's easy money. easy, right. I put in my first £12,000 in March 2021, blew half of it on ads and the other half on laptop stands that nobody wanted. took me a good year to figure out what I was doing. Robbo runs our warehouse now, actually, so it all worked out. he still reminds me about the laptop stands every Christmas party.

\[00:02:41\] **Who's on the team now, and who does what?**

so, the books are done by Sarah Whitcombe, she's technically freelance but she's basically ours. honestly, without Sarah's spreadsheets we'd have gone under in the first year. Rob runs the warehouse with two lads on packing. sourcing in China goes through Wei Lin, he's an agent based in Shenzhen, been there about twelve years, deals with all the factories for us. on the US side we've got a bookkeeper too, Karen Morrison, she does the LLC's taxes. and me, I do listings, ads, cash, arguing with suppliers, all the rest of it. director, marketer, occasionally the cleaner.

\[00:04:02\] **Tell me more about sourcing. How does working with Wei actually go?**

it's all trust, really. I send Wei what I want, links, photos, rough target price, he goes out to the factory, checks samples, haggles. usually the minimum order is about $4,500, sometimes more for bigger items. he takes 5 per cent of the order value. Wei's old school, doesn't like email much, he'd rather just ring you. I've got his UK number saved because he's over here a few times a year, 07700 900417. the frustrating bit is when he goes quiet for a week and you've no idea whether the goods have shipped, and meanwhile your ads are running and orders are coming in.

\[00:05:33\] **What's the most painful part of the whole chain?**

freight, without a doubt. we used to use Pellow Freight Ltd, then we left because they lost a container on us, roughly 40k worth of stock. I spent six months emailing their account manager, Dave Morrison. and before you ask, no relation to Karen, it's just a common name, they've never met. different Morrison entirely. anyway, Dave kept telling me it was stuck in customs, then that it was sitting in a depot in Felixstowe, then he just stopped replying. in the end they refunded 30% and only after a formal complaint and a solicitor's letter.

\[00:07:15\] **Who did you move to after that?**

we're with Northgate Shipping Ltd now, the operations lead is Grace Okafor, really sharp. you can actually talk to Grace, she answers on weekends even. I can give you her details if you want to interview her as well, email's grace.okafor@example.com and her mobile is +44 7700 900982. tell her Tom sent you and she'll pick up. their office number is 020 7946 0381 but nobody ever answers that.

\[00:08:30\] **How do you work out the economics of a single order?**

that's all in Sarah's spreadsheet. landed cost with freight, duty, certification, marketplace fees, all of it. so a chopping board might cost us £3.20 landed, we sell it at £19.99, but then there's the 15% referral fee, fulfilment fees, returns, ads. we clear maybe three or four quid a unit on a good day. last month turnover was about £210,000 and what actually stayed in the bank was more like twenty grand. January we basically broke even. I honestly don't know where the money goes until Sarah sits me down and walks me through it.

\[00:10:05\] **You mentioned the US company. How was setting that up?**

painful. lots of forms. for the LLC they wanted my personal details for the bank and the tax side, so I was reading my SSN out over the phone to some bloke at the formation agency, 767-34-7863, and my UK National Insurance number as well, SH 37 76 29 D, because they needed proof of identity from both sides. and I'm sat there thinking, who exactly am I reading this out to? turned out fine, but still. the registered agent is in Austin, and Karen handles the filings from Dallas. her number's (214) 555-0143 if you ever need a US accountant, she's brilliant.

\[00:11:48\] **And how's the relationship with the marketplaces themselves?**

fees and fines. on the 5th of March we got hit with a £600 charge because a carton was two centimetres over the size limit. two centimetres. and you write to seller support and get a bot sending you templates. then there's inbound: you book a slot at the fulfilment centre, the lorry turns up and they turn it away, and you pay for the wait. Shopify's nicer in that sense, it's our own store, but sales there are maybe a fifth of Amazon. so there's not much choice really. and the rules change every month, that's what kills you.

\[00:13:20\] **How do you find new products these days?**

analytics tools, mostly, you can see what's trending. plus Wei sends me stuff he spots at trade fairs in Shenzhen and Guangzhou, the Canton Fair runs twice a year. he's going in April, I've already given him a list of about thirty items. Robbo throws ideas in as well, more gadgets, but he's got a good eye. the hard part isn't finding a product, it's the timing. by the time stock lands two months later the niche is rammed. happened with water bottles, we were three weeks too late.

\[00:15:02\] **Do you have an office, or is everyone remote?**

there's a small office in Leeds, it's really just a desk in a co-working space. and we've got a tiny admin office in Harrogate, one person doing invoices and paperwork, she's the only bookkeeper at our Harrogate branch, Sarah supervises her remotely. why Harrogate? cheap rent and we found a good person, that's literally it. the warehouse, as I said, is outside Bradford, that's Rob's kingdom.

\[00:16:28\] **How does the team communicate? Which tools?**

WhatsApp, mostly. one big group, everyone dumps everything in there, photos, invoices, memes. Rob posts photos of damaged deliveries. sometimes he messages at two in the morning, the lorry's in and half the boxes are crushed. Sarah prefers email, her work address is s.whitcombe@example.net, she keeps all the invoices there, says things get lost in WhatsApp. and spreadsheets, obviously. you've got my number, but just in case, 07700 900526, that's the main one.

\[00:18:10\] **Were there disputes with contractors that really hurt the business?**

the freight thing was the big one. when that container went missing I genuinely thought we were done. loan to repay, no stock, bad reviews piling up. what saved us was a solicitor, J. T. Fairbairn, from Fairbairn & Cole LLP in Manchester. he drafted the complaint and the letter before action, never went to court. we paid Fairbairn about £2,800 and it was the best money we spent that year. he said Pellow had a whole stack of cases like ours, people just don't bother suing. and then there was the factory that sent spice racks without the screws, Wei went over there himself and shouted at them for half a day.

\[00:19:50\] **Who makes the financial decisions?**

me. well, formally me, but no payment goes out without Sarah signing it off. on paper she's down as S. Whitcombe, responsible for accounts, she's got bank access. I call her Ms Whitcombe when she's telling me off for overspending. for sourcing I've got a separate card, 4000 3480 7697 1170, Wei invoices against it and Sarah reconciles. anything big, like a new order over fifty grand, the three of us talk it through, me, Sarah and Rob, because he's the one who has to find space for it.

\[00:21:15\] **How much time a week goes on routine work you'd like to hand off?**

loads. twenty hours, maybe. reports, reconciliations, replying to reviews, rewriting listings. reviews are their own nightmare, dozens a day, and you have to answer or the rating drops. I tried giving it to a freelancer and he made it worse. now I do some myself and an AI tool does the rest. Sarah does the reports, but she's got a couple of other clients too, so she can't do everything.

\[00:22:35\] **Have you tried giving reports or spreadsheets to an AI tool?**

I have, yeah. and honestly that's where the paranoia kicks in. once I dropped our payroll sheet into a chatbot so it would work out the quarterly cost. full names, NI numbers, salaries, the lot. it did the maths beautifully, and then I sat there thinking, so where does all that live now? Sarah nearly killed me when she found out. she said, you know that's personal data, there are fines for that. Rob Ashdown's got a worse story, he uploaded a supplier chat and the supplier's passport scan was in the attachments. nobody found out, but still.

\[00:24:20\] **What would you want a tool like that to do?**

drop in a spreadsheet or a document, it strips out the names, numbers, phone numbers, gives me something clean. then when the AI answers, it puts everything back, so I'm not sitting there working out who PERSON_3 is. and it has to run on my laptop, no cloud, otherwise what's the point. and it mustn't touch the numbers. if it swaps £210,000 for some placeholder, I don't want it, the numbers are the whole point. same with dates, I need to know a shipment landed on 14 February, not just at some point.

\[00:25:35\] **How do you hire people? Where do you find them?**

mostly through people we know, to be honest. we tried job boards, you get people who leave after a month. Rob brought in both his packers, they'd worked together before. our newest listings person, Hannah Pryor, came through a friend of a friend in Manchester, she works remotely, does the listings and edits the photos. Hannah's got a real eye for design, listings sell maybe twenty per cent better after she's touched them. Sarah handles all the contracts, she knows what paperwork's needed, I don't go near it. and there's a one-month probation, if someone hasn't clicked by then they never will, in my experience.

\[00:27:05\] **Where do you keep staff documents?**

oh. this is the embarrassing bit. some of it's in a shared drive, in a folder called HR, some of it's on Sarah's laptop, and some of it's just in WhatsApp. when Hannah joined she dropped her passport scan straight into the group chat, and I think it's still sitting there, nobody ever deleted it. Sarah keeps the signed contracts and the originals. I know it's not how it should be, but when there's seven of you, you don't really think about policies. if someone came along and said, here's how you do it, here's the button, I'd do it. I just don't have the time to work it out myself.

\[00:28:30\] **Have you ever been audited?**

once, in 2024. we got a letter from HMRC asking us to explain some VAT figures on returns, something didn't add up. Sarah spent two days pulling the paperwork together, it all checked out in the end, but we still paid a £400 penalty for filing something late. I gave her a raise afterwards, honestly. there was another time when stock arrived without the right labelling, but that was the marketplace fining us, not the government. lots of stress, lots of money, nothing to show for it.

\[00:30:00\] **Where do you see the business in a year?**

I want a second warehouse, probably near York, closer to the north-east customers, freight works out cheaper. and my wife, Emma, wants her own line, kids' stuff, she says I know nothing about it and she's right. Em's already looking at suppliers, through Wei as well. if it works out it'll be a separate company in her name. Robbo says I've lost my mind, but he says that about every idea I have and then copies it six months later. and I'd really like to get the paperwork sorted so I'm not embarrassed by it.

\[00:31:25\] **Who else do you know that might be interested?**

Robbo, definitely, he's mentioned it himself. there's also Niamh Brennan in Belfast, she imports textiles, runs Brennan Linen Ltd, about twenty staff, all the HR stuff lives in spreadsheets. her number's +44 28 9649 6012, tell her I sent you. and I'd talk to the woman in Northgate's purchasing team who won their supplier-of-the-year thing last year, she's very organised. oh, and our forklift driver, the one who ran the London Marathon dressed as a dinosaur, he keeps the shift rota in spreadsheets as well.

\[00:33:00\] **Last question. What would you pay for something like that?**

depends how well it works. if it really saves time and I'm not worried about the data, twenty, thirty quid a month, easy. with an Amazon integration so reports come out clean straight away, fifty would be fine. for comparison, I spend about $120 a month on analytics and I think that's steep.

\[00:33:45\] **Thanks, Tom. Can I come back to you in a month with a prototype?**

yeah, of course. message me or call +44 7700 900526, same number, I just say it differently every time. not Mondays though, Monday's inbound day, I'm at the warehouse with Rob all day. and do get in touch with Grace Okafor, seriously, she'll tell you loads about freight.
